catalog_quote: Distinctions from Suprasegmental Features. By suprasegmental features here we refer basically to the use of tones. With the old system, there was virtually no use of tones. There is the use of tones with the new system. Several domains of tonal contrast can be used to illustrate the distinctive role of tones in the language to show the relevance of the new alphabet adapted from the GACL. This has to do with contrast between lexical items and grammatical functions in the language like in marking tenses. new_statements.quote: By suprasegmental features here we refer basically to the use of tones. With the old system, there was virtually no use of tones. [...] In Engwo, the contrastive function of tones can be illustrated in six different areas. These include (i) contrast between lexical items, (ii) marking of preposition, (iii) indicating the agent or possessor, (iv) marking the diminutive, (v) marking tenses, and (vi) making distinctions between pronouns [p. 363] ... Lexical contrastive features like vowel length, vowel nasalisation and grammatical distinctions like tense which are marked by tone need to be distinguished in Cameroonian languages like Engwo. PDF p. 9 (printed p. 367, CONCLUSION) gives, verba…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngwo/Engwo is a register tone language (H, M, L level tones, LH and HL contours; mid tone unmarked in the orthography) in which tone carries the lexical and grammatical contrasts; the author treats the language's suprasegmentals as 'basically' tone and mentions stress only as a property of European languages. No placement rule for word stress is stated and no source examined asserts or denies word-level stress outright.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the article is an orthography justification, not a phonological description, and contains no stress data.
new_statements.domain_note: Examples are isolated nouns, noun-plus-preposition phrases, and short clauses; tone alternations are shown at word and phrase level ('post morphemic and post lexical constructions'). Neither the old nor new orthography marks intonation (p. 365).
new_statements.identity_note: Eyoh 2021 describes Engwo/Ngwo as a 'language unit' of nine dialects (Bako, Bakwa/Okorobi, Banya, Basa, Ekwebo, Ikweri, Konda, Ngwo, Amasi) and writes about the standard Engwo orthography for the whole unit; Glottolog ngwo1241 has dialects basa1285, kond1300, nucl1414 etc. and treats Amasi as a separate language (Momo). Eyoh's data represent the Ngwo (nuclear) variety of Njikwa; no dialect is singled out.

new_statements.quote: There are five phonemic tones in Engwo but only three are marked on words. The mid tone and the low-high tone are left unmarked. The various tones include: The high tone (á) as in étáa "heart" / The low tone (à) as in ètàn "grasshoppers" / The mid tone (ā) as in etan "on the bed" / The falling tone (â) as in gô "mahogany tree" / The rising tone (ǎ) as in go "fall" [...] It is good to master the tones very well. If you use the wrong tone, you get a wrong word which gives the wrong message.
new_statements.citation: Eyoh, Julius A. 2018. Notes on Phonology and Orthography / Notes on Engwo Grammar. Engwo (Ngwo) Dictionary, Webonary (SIL Global). https://www.webonary.org/engwo/language/phonology/

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing statement from Eyoh 2021 (tone language, contrastive lexical tone, no stress statement); the catalog record for Engwo has an empty rule, and this source gives nothing to fill it with. Adds detail on the tone inventory (five tones vs. the three level tones plus contours in Eyoh 2021).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Engwo is described as having five phonemic tones (high, low, mid, falling, rising), marked also on syllabic nasals and split across long vowels; the page says nothing about word stress, accent or prominence (a full-text search for stress/accent the phonology page and of the companion 'Notes on Engwo Grammar' page finds no occurrence of stress/accent/prominence).
new_statements.exceptions: none (tone only; mid and rising tones are unmarked in the orthography)
new_statements.identity_note: Eyoh 2018 describes the Engwo (Ngwo) variety standardized by the Ngwo community at Sabli-Ngwo (alphabet adopted 7 July 2007); no dialect distinctions are drawn. The listed theses concern Ngwo of Cameroon per their titles (Glottolog language code ngn).

sources.locator: p. 363, section 'Distinctions from Suprasegmental Features' (PDF p. 5); contrast with European stress on p. 367, 'Conclusion' (PDF p. 9)
sources.note: Orthography article by the native-speaker linguist who compiled the lexicon and wrote the 2015 PhD. Section 'Distinctions from Suprasegmental Features' (pp. 363-365): 'By suprasegmental features here we refer basically to the use of tones'; three level tones H/M/L plus LH and HL contours, mid tone left unmarked; six contrastive functions of tone (lexical, preposition, possessor, diminutive, tense, pronoun). No statement about word stress; the conclusion (p. 367) contrasts these tonal contrasts with 'stress patterns in European languages'; p. 365 notes neither alphabet marks intonation.
